title: The Verge: a Wall Street lawyer, his brother's agency, and six years of American foreign policy
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Manse and the Grandfather's Trade

stops.name: Washington, birth into the office
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is born in his grandfather's city, into a family that treats the State Department as a trade. John Watson Foster, Secretary of State to Benjamin Harrison, is the grandfather; Robert Lansing, who will hold the same office under Wilson, marries in as an uncle. The father, Allen Macy Dulles, is a Presbyterian minister who intends his eldest son for the pulpit. The boy is given the grandfather's name. The household soon moves north to a manse in Watertown, New York, where four more children will follow.
suggested_refs: The Foster house in Washington, seat of a family that produced three Secretaries of State in three generations
sources: history.state.gov, Office of the Historian, biographical register

stops.name: Watertown, the minister's five children
stops.date_confidence: attested for the household; the date is Allen's birth, used to fix the family at Watertown
stops.campa: The manse holds a minister, his wife, and five children taught at home because their parents distrust the public schools. Allen Dulles is born here in 1893, five years behind his brother; Eleanor follows. Mornings run on scripture. At the table the children are made to use French and German, and nobody states as a rule the thing the whole house knows, that this family produces men who serve the government. Foster is the eldest and the quickest. His father intends him for the ministry.
suggested_refs: The Presbyterian manse at Watertown, New York, boyhood house of both Dulles brothers
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, 'Watertown, birth in the manse' (canonical pin inherited)

stops.name: The Hague, secretary to the Chinese delegation
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Second Hague Peace Conference ran 15 June to 18 October 1907
stops.campa: At nineteen he crosses to the Netherlands as secretary to his grandfather, who sits at the Second Hague Peace Conference not for the United States but as retained counsel to the Chinese delegation under Lu Zhengxiang. From June to October the delegates argue arbitration, the laws of naval war, and the collection of contract debts by force, in a thirteenth-century hall built for a count. The boy carries papers and watches a former Secretary of State work for a foreign government on a fee. He is back at Princeton by autumn.
suggested_refs: The Ridderzaal in the Binnenhof, seat of the Second Hague Peace Conference, 1907
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907' (corrects the common claim that Foster attended for the United States)

stops.name: Princeton, the degree and the society
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the June commencement date is conventional
stops.campa: He takes his degree at twenty, Phi Beta Kappa, after four years of arguing in the American Whig-Cliosophic Society. Allen Dulles will enter this same college and this same society six years behind him, and from then on the brothers' addresses repeat each other: one Wall Street firm, one peace conference in Paris, one wartime board, and at the end a government they run between them by telephone. His father still expects a seminary to follow the degree. He goes to Washington and enrolls in law.
suggested_refs: The American Whig-Cliosophic Society at Princeton, debating society of both brothers
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, 'Princeton, Nassau Hall and the class of 1914' (canonical pin inherited)

stops.name: George Washington University, reading law
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the law course runs from about 1908, the bar and the move to New York are dated 1911; month and day unknown
stops.campa: He reads law at George Washington University, a few blocks from the department his grandfather once ran and his uncle Robert Lansing will run within five years. What the classroom does not teach him the family table does: treaties, arbitration, indemnities, the mechanics of getting a foreign government to put its name on a paper. He passes the bar and takes the train to New York, intending to practice international law and nothing else. In 1911 international law is barely a practice at all. He is twenty-three.
suggested_refs: George Washington University Law School, Washington, D.C.

stops.name: 48 Wall Street, Sullivan and Cromwell
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1911; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Sullivan and Cromwell takes him into its international department, and he does not leave the firm for forty-two years. Family connection opens the door; what keeps him there is a talent for the specific work of moving capital across borders under law, at the moment American money begins to do that at scale. He will make name partner, then head of the firm. His younger brother joins him here in 1926, and through the interwar decades the two of them arrange German bond issues.
suggested_refs: Sullivan and Cromwell at 48 Wall Street, the firm both Dulles brothers served
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, '48 Wall Street, joining his brother's firm' (canonical pin inherited)

stops.name: Auburn, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the 26 June date rests on secondary sources only
stops.campa: He marries Janet Pomeroy Avery in her family's town in the Finger Lakes. Her grandfather Theodore Pomeroy had been Speaker of the House of Representatives for a single day, at the close of the Fortieth Congress. They will have three children. The marriage runs forty-seven years and ends at Walter Reed. She travels with him on the missions of the last decade and stands at the back of the delegation photographs. What she made of any of it the reachable record does not say.
suggested_refs: Theodore M. Pomeroy, Speaker of the House for one day, 3 March 1869

stops.name: San Jose, the isthmus and the war
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1917; month and day not fixed by the sources reached
stops.campa: Rejected for the Army over his eyesight, he is sent to Central America by his uncle, now Secretary of State, to keep the isthmus out of German hands. In Costa Rica he argues for supporting Federico Tinoco, who took the country by coup that January; in Nicaragua, for Emiliano Chamorro. The declared American interest is the canal and the denial of ports and cable stations to Germany, and how a government came by its power is not among the questions asked. The recommendations go out over his uncle's name. He is twenty-nine and holds no office in the government.
suggested_refs: The Tinoco regime in Costa Rica, 1917-1919, and the question of United States recognition

stops.name: Washington, the War Trade Board
stops.date_confidence: inferred: service dated to 1917-1918; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Commissioned a major, he serves on the War Trade Board, the body that licenses every export leaving the United States and decides which neutral firms may receive American goods. It is economic warfare conducted as paperwork: blacklists, quotas, cotton and copper withheld from companies suspected of transshipping to Germany. He is thirty, and this is the second time he has worked inside the executive branch without being confirmed to anything. The board dissolves with the armistice.
suggested_refs: The United States War Trade Board, 1917-1919, and the blacklist system

stops.name: Paris, the Crillon and the reparations clauses
stops.date_confidence: attested: the conference opens 18 January 1919; the delegation occupies the Crillon from December 1918
stops.campa: The American delegation takes over the Hotel de Crillon on the Place de la Concorde, and both Dulles brothers arrive with it on their first shared assignment: Foster as legal counsel on reparations under Bernard Baruch, Allen on boundary questions, both of them nephews of the Secretary of State. Foster argues against the sums the French and British want, on the ground that a figure Germany cannot pay is a figure that will not be paid. He loses the argument and drafts the clauses anyway. The signing in June happens at Versailles, twelve miles west; the work is done here, in a hotel on a square.
suggested_refs: The American Commission to Negotiate Peace at the Hotel de Crillon, 1919
The Reparations Commission and Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, 'Paris, the delegation at the Crillon' (canonical pin inherited)

stops.name: London, the Dawes Plan and the circuit of dollars
stops.date_confidence: attested: the London Conference concluded 16 August 1924
stops.campa: The settlement he warned against has collapsed, French troops are in the Ruhr, and the mark is worthless. The remedy, negotiated at the London Conference and named for the Chicago banker who chaired the committee, is to lend Germany the money to pay the reparations, in dollars, raised on the American market. Dulles is at the center of the legal work. Through the rest of the decade Sullivan and Cromwell places on the order of a billion dollars of foreign bonds, a large share of them German. New York lends, Germany pays London and Paris, London and Paris pay New York.
suggested_refs: The Dawes Plan of 1924 and the American loan flotation that carried it

stops.name: 48 Wall Street, his brother comes to the firm
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1926; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Allen Dulles resigns from the Foreign Service and joins his brother's firm, on the plain ground that a diplomat's salary will not keep a family. For fifteen years the two work the same corridor: bond issues for German municipalities and German industry, cartel agreements, the incorporation of foreign subsidiaries. Foster is the senior man and the better lawyer; Allen is the better company and knows more people. Both belong to the Council on Foreign Relations. Both have their names on the German loans.
suggested_refs: Sullivan and Cromwell's interwar German bond practice
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, '48 Wall Street, joining his brother's firm'

stops.name: Berlin, the clients who do not change
stops.date_confidence: inferred: repeated visits across the 1920s and into the 1930s; no single trip fixed by the sources reached
stops.campa: He comes to Berlin repeatedly through the twenties and into the thirties for the firm's German practice: loans to municipalities, to the steel combines, to the chemical trust, and the international nickel cartel into which the firm helped fit I.G. Farben. The clients do not change when the government does. Sullivan and Cromwell keeps its Berlin office and a Frankfurt subsidiary open through the first two years of the Nazi state, and the letterhead of an American law firm goes on appearing over German paper into 1935.
suggested_refs: Sullivan and Cromwell's Berlin office and Frankfurt subsidiary, closed 1935
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, 'Berlin, the office closed and the date moved' (canonical pin inherited)

stops.name: 48 Wall Street, the vote he loses
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1935; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: His brother comes back from Germany having seen what is being done to German Jews and moves that the firm close Berlin and Frankfurt. The partners vote for it. Foster votes against, alone, and loses; the firm afterward dates the closure announcement to 1934, a year earlier than the vote. He is forty-seven, at the head of the most profitable international practice in New York, and his position is that a law firm is not a government and does not conduct foreign policy. The Berlin and Frankfurt offices close.
stops.quote: Over the sole opposition of Allen's brother and fellow partner, John Foster Dulles, the firm's partners voted in 1935 to close the Berlin office and a subsidiary in Frankfurt.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Sullivan & Cromwell' (a third-party statement about Dulles, not his own words)
suggested_refs: The 1935 partners' vote at Sullivan and Cromwell and the backdated closure announcement
sources: Note: the same encyclopedia elsewhere states the firm assisted the German arms buildup by incorporating I.G. Farben into an international nickel cartel; the tension is left unresolved

segments.name: Six Pillars, and Four Months in the Senate

stops.name: New York, the Commission on a Just and Durable Peace
stops.date_confidence: attested: appointed to the commission December 1940, the Six Pillars statement published March 1943
stops.campa: Chairing the Federal Council of Churches commission since December 1940, he publishes the Six Pillars of Peace: a Protestant program for the postwar world calling for continuing collaboration among the United Nations, treaty revision by process rather than by war, an international organization with real authority, autonomy for subject peoples, and religious and intellectual liberty. The argument is for a federation of states standing above states. He is read as a churchman in these years. The statement goes out under his name in March 1943.
suggested_refs: Six Pillars of Peace (Federal Council of Churches, March 1943)

stops.name: San Francisco, the preamble at the opera house
stops.date_confidence: attested: the conference opens 25 April 1945
stops.campa: He comes to the founding conference as adviser to Senator Arthur Vandenberg, the Republican who has to be kept aboard if the Senate is going to ratify anything, and works on the language of the Charter's preamble. He will stand in this same hall in six years, on the other side of the table, to make a peace with Japan. Fifty nations sign in June. The building is a municipal opera house with the seats left in, the delegates down in the stalls and the press up in the boxes.
suggested_refs: The War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco, venue of the 1945 United Nations Conference on International Organization

stops.name: The Capitol, four months as a senator
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Thomas Dewey, for whom Dulles has written the foreign policy of two presidential campaigns and who would have made him Secretary of State had either been won, appoints him to a vacant New York seat in the Senate. He is sworn in on the seventh of July, holds the seat through the summer and autumn, and loses the November special election to Herbert Lehman. Fourteen months after the defeat a Democratic administration hires him to write the peace with Japan. It is the only time in his life he stands before voters.
suggested_refs: The 1949 New York special Senate election, Dulles against Herbert Lehman

stops.name: Washington, the appointment and War or Peace
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1950; the April date of the State Department appointment rests on secondary sources
stops.campa: Dean Acheson brings him into the department as special adviser on the Japanese settlement, an appointment made across party lines in an election year and attacked from both sides for it. He is sixty-two and has never run anything larger than a law firm. The same season he publishes War or Peace, an attack on containment as a doctrine that concedes the initiative and the map: the object should not be to hold a line but to work toward the liberation of the countries already behind it. Macmillan prints it in 1950 and it sells.
suggested_refs: John Foster Dulles, War or Peace (Macmillan, 1950)

stops.name: Tokyo, the Dai-ichi building
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1950-1951 negotiating missions; the January 1951 arrival is the best-dated of them
stops.campa: He arrives in an occupied capital to write a peace postponed five years, and works against the headquarters in the Dai-ichi Life building where MacArthur sits, a block of insurance offices facing the palace moat. What he designs is unusual for being generous: no reparations of consequence, no continued Allied control, sovereignty returned whole. The price is written in a second document. Japan will host American forces indefinitely and will make its foreign policy in consultation with Washington. He negotiates the two treaties as one instrument.
suggested_refs: The Dai-ichi Life Insurance Building (DN Tower 21), Tokyo, seat of GHQ-SCAP

stops.name: The Presidio, ANZUS and the second treaty
stops.date_confidence: attested: ANZUS signed 1 September 1951, the bilateral security treaty 8 September, both at the Presidio
stops.campa: A week before the peace treaty, at the Presidio, the ANZUS pact is signed with Australia and New Zealand: the price those two governments set for accepting a soft peace with the country that bombed Darwin and took Singapore. Seven days later, in an officers' club on the same post, the bilateral security treaty with Japan is signed a few hours after the peace treaty itself. American forces stay on Japanese soil for a term the document does not fix.
suggested_refs: The ANZUS Treaty, signed at San Francisco 1 September 1951
The Security Treaty between the United States and Japan, signed at the Presidio 8 September 1951

stops.name: San Francisco, the treaty and the island it does not name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Forty-eight nations sign the Treaty of San Francisco in the hall where the United Nations Charter was drafted six years earlier. The Soviet Union, Poland, and Czechoslovakia attend and refuse to sign. Neither Chinese government is invited, and the treaty has Japan renounce all right and title to Formosa and the Pescadores without naming who receives them. The omission is his own drafting and it is not an oversight; no formula existed that Washington, London, Taipei, and Peking could all be brought to. Four years later he says of it only that Japan merely renounced sovereignty over Taiwan.
stops.quote: Japan merely renounced sovereignty over Taiwan
stops.quote_source: Dulles, statement of 1955, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Treaty of San Francisco'; continued in the same source as the United States 'cannot, therefore, admit that the disposition of Taiwan is merely an internal problem of China'
suggested_refs: The Treaty of San Francisco, 8 September 1951, and the undetermined status of Taiwan

stops.name: The State Department, sworn in
stops.date_confidence: attested by history.state.gov as appointment and entry on duty, 21 January 1953; a widely repeated account gives 26 January, and the atlas file for his brother follows that second date. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved
stops.campa: The Senate confirms him and he enters on duty the day after the inauguration, at sixty-four, in the office his grandfather held under Harrison and his uncle under Wilson. He is the third of his family in the room. On the twenty-sixth of February his brother Allen becomes Director of Central Intelligence, and for six years the open and the covert instruments of American foreign policy are directed by two sons of the Watertown manse who can settle a question between them by telephone with nothing written down. Their sister Eleanor is in the building too, on the German desk.
suggested_refs: history.state.gov, Secretaries of State: John Foster Dulles, 1953-1959
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, 'The White House, the two brothers sworn in' (dates the oath to 26 January)

stops.name: The State Department, the order for Tehran
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coup; the American authorization is dated to spring and summer 1953 without a single fixed date in the sources reached
stops.campa: He does not go to Tehran. The operation against Mohammad Mosaddegh, who nationalized the Anglo-Iranian oil concession two years earlier, is set in motion from Washington in the spring, run out of the Tehran station by Kermit Roosevelt, and carried through the streets on the nineteenth of August by crowds that were paid to be there. Dulles supplies the policy, the diplomatic cover, and the handling of the British; the cables and the money are his brother's department. The Shah, who had flown to Rome, comes back.
suggested_refs: Operation TPAJAX and the declassified CIA internal history of the Iran coup
sources: allen_dulles.journey.json, '2430 E Street, the order for Tehran'

stops.name: New York, massive retaliatory power
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He goes to the Council on Foreign Relations, an institution he has belonged to for thirty years, to explain the administration's military doctrine. Conventional defense everywhere is unaffordable and will break the budget before it deters anyone; therefore the response to aggression will come at places and by means of American choosing, with nuclear weapons behind it. He never says massive retaliation. He says massive retaliatory power, and the newspapers supply the shorter phrase inside a week.
stops.quote: Local defense will always be important. But there is no local defense which alone will contain the mighty land power of the Communist world. Local defenses must be reinforced by the further deterrent of massive retaliatory power. A potential aggressor must know that he cannot always prescribe battle conditions that suit him.
stops.quote_source: Speech to the Council on Foreign Relations, 12 January 1954, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Massive retaliation'
suggested_refs: The Harold Pratt House, 58 East 68th Street, home of the Council on Foreign Relations since 1945
sources: Wikipedia, 'Massive retaliation' (which notes the literal phrase is not his)

stops.name: London, the bombers Churchill refuses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the April 1954 London mission; the plan itself dates from March 1954
stops.campa: The French garrison at Dien Bien Phu has been under siege since March and will not hold. Admiral Radford's plan, worked up at French request, calls for as many as ninety-eight B-29s from Okinawa and the Philippines with carrier fighters over them, and carries an option for three small atomic weapons. Eisenhower will not move without allies. Dulles crosses to London to get Churchill and Eden, and Churchill declines; the British will not go to war to hold French Indochina. Eisenhower cancels the operation.
suggested_refs: Operation Vulture, March-April 1954, and the British refusal of united action
sources: Wikipedia, 'Operation Vulture' (correcting both the March origin and the attribution to the Air Force)

stops.name: Geneva, one week at the Palais des Nations
stops.date_confidence: attested: Dulles at Geneva 26 April to 3 May 1954 only; the conference itself ran to 21 July
stops.campa: He leads the American delegation for one week and forbids his staff any contact with the Chinese. When Zhou Enlai puts out a hand in a corridor he does not take it, a refusal told and retold in Peking for thirty years afterward. On the third of May he goes home and leaves Walter Bedell Smith to sit through the rest. The partition at the seventeenth parallel and the reunification elections promised for 1956 are settled in July, when he is a continent away, and it falls to Bedell Smith to say that the United States will not sign.
suggested_refs: The 1954 Geneva Conference on Korea and Indochina, Palais des Nations
sources: Wikipedia, '1954 Geneva Conference' (correcting the common claim that Dulles stayed through July)

stops.name: The State Department, the old client in Guatemala
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Jacobo Arbenz's land reform has expropriated uncultivated acreage from the United Fruit Company, which was a Sullivan and Cromwell client and for which both brothers had done work. On the eighteenth of June some four hundred men cross from Honduras behind a radio station and a handful of unmarked aircraft, and the object is not to win a war but to persuade the Guatemalan army that it is losing one. Arbenz resigns on the twenty-seventh. Dulles tells the press the bombing was the work of the Guatemalan air force.
suggested_refs: Operation PBSUCCESS and the declassified CIA record of the 1954 Guatemalan coup
sources: Wikipedia, '1954 Guatemalan coup d'etat' (the air force claim is the encyclopedia's paraphrase, not a located verbatim statement; treated as reconstruction)
allen_dulles.journey.json, 'The White House, the plan for Guatemala'

stops.name: Manila, the pact and its missing members
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eight weeks after Geneva he assembles at Manila the treaty organization meant to hold the line the conference drew. The signatories are the United States, Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Thailand, and Pakistan; two of the eight are Southeast Asian states. A protocol extends the pact's cover to Laos, Cambodia, and the southern half of Vietnam, all three of which the Geneva accords barred from joining any alliance. The organization is given no standing forces and no unified command.
suggested_refs: The Manila Pact of 8 September 1954 and the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization
sources: Wikipedia, 'Southeast Asia Treaty Organization' (coordinate correction for Manila)

stops.name: The State Department, the treaty with Taipei
stops.date_confidence: attested: signed at Washington 2 December 1954, in force 3 March 1955
stops.campa: He signs with the Republic of China's foreign minister a mutual defense treaty covering Taiwan and the Pescadores, in Washington, not in Taipei. The islands the treaty does not name are Quemoy and Matsu, a few miles off the mainland coast and garrisoned by a third of Chiang Kai-shek's army; the omission is deliberate. Peking is meant to be unable to calculate what the United States would do. An exchange of notes attached to the treaty restrains Chiang from attacking the mainland without American consent.
suggested_refs: The Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty, Washington, 2 December 1954
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty' (correcting the frequent placement of the signing in Taipei)

stops.name: Ames, neutrality called immoral
stops.date_confidence: contested: the sentence is dated 9 June 1955 in some sources and to a June 1956 Iowa State College commencement in others; the place is standard attribution and could not be resolved against a transcript
stops.campa: Speaking to a graduating class in Iowa, he says that neutrality has increasingly become obsolete and, outside very exceptional circumstances, is an immoral and shortsighted conception. He means India, Egypt, Indonesia, and the bloc that has just met at Bandung, and the sentence is read in Delhi exactly as it sounds. Twelve years earlier the same man chaired a commission of churches arguing that the moral unit of politics is not the nation. He never explains the distance between the two positions.
stops.quote: Neutrality has increasingly become obsolete and, except under very exceptional circumstances, it is an immoral and shortsighted conception.
stops.quote_source: Dulles, speech of 9 June 1955, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'John Foster Dulles'
suggested_refs: The Bandung Conference of April 1955 and the emergence of the nonaligned bloc
sources: Note: the pool of gathered sources tags this item [R] and records the 1955/1956 date conflict unresolved

stops.name: Washington, the word that sticks
stops.date_confidence: attested: Life magazine, 16 January 1956
stops.campa: James Shepley of Life publishes an interview in which the Secretary counts three occasions, Korea, Indochina, and the Taiwan Strait, on which he says he carried the United States deliberately to the edge of war and got what he wanted without going over. Allied governments read the piece and are not comforted to learn how near they had been taken without being told. Adlai Stevenson, running against the administration that year, turns the phrase into a noun and uses it against him: brinkmanship.
stops.quote: The ability to get to the verge without getting into the war is the necessary art.
stops.quote_source: James R. Shepley, 'How Dulles Averted War,' Life, 16 January 1956, p. 70ff.
suggested_refs: Life magazine, 16 January 1956, the Shepley interview that produced the term brinkmanship
sources: Wikiquote, 'John Foster Dulles' (independent confirmation of the wording)

stops.name: The State Department, the dam withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He calls in the Egyptian ambassador, Ahmed Hussein, and tells him the United States is withdrawing from the financing of the High Dam at Aswan. The stated ground is Egypt's capacity to pay; the working grounds include the arms Nasser bought from Czechoslovakia the previous autumn and his recognition of Peking. Britain withdraws behind him and the World Bank follows. On the twenty-sixth, in Alexandria, Nasser nationalizes the Suez Canal Company in the middle of a speech, and the crowd hears the code word before the sentence ends.
suggested_refs: The withdrawal of Aswan High Dam financing, 19 July 1956, and Nasser's Alexandria speech of 26 July
sources: Wikipedia, 'Suez Crisis' (correcting the frequent placement of this scene in Cairo)

stops.name: London, the conference that buys time
stops.date_confidence: attested for the London conference of 16-23 August 1956
stops.campa: Twenty-two maritime nations meet in London over the canal, and Dulles arrives with a proposal for an international board to run it, then with a users' association, then with the offer of another conference. Eden and Mollet want the thing settled by force and read every American instrument as a delaying tactic. It is a delaying tactic. His object is to keep them from shooting until the crisis cools. Whether he ever told them in plain words that the United States would oppose an invasion is not settled by the record.
suggested_refs: The London Conference on the Suez Canal, August 1956, and the Suez Canal Users Association

stops.name: Walter Reed, the first operation
stops.date_confidence: attested for early November 1956; the exact date of admission varies between accounts
stops.campa: On the third of November, with British and French aircraft over Egyptian airfields and Soviet tanks in Budapest, he is taken to Walter Reed in the night with severe abdominal pain. The surgeons find a perforation and a cancer of the colon and take out part of the bowel. He is out of the government for weeks, through the worst crisis of his tenure, and Eisenhower forces the British and French withdrawal himself, working the telephone from the White House. Dulles is sixty-eight. He will be under treatment for this disease for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The old Walter Reed Army Medical Center campus on Georgia Avenue NW, closed 2011
sources: Wikipedia, 'Walter Reed Army Medical Center' (coordinate correction)

stops.name: The State Department, nuclear weapons on the table for Kinmen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2 September 1958 meeting with the Joint Chiefs
stops.campa: The People's Liberation Army has been shelling Kinmen since the twenty-third of August, tens of thousands of rounds a day onto an island a few miles off the mainland with a large part of Chiang's army on it. On the second of September Dulles meets the Joint Chiefs. Nuclear strikes against mainland airfields are weighed in the room, to be used if conventional resupply of the island fails. The decision is conventional means first, and eight-inch howitzers and escorted convoys do the work. Nothing about the nuclear option is said in public.
suggested_refs: The Second Taiwan Strait Crisis, 23 August to 2 December 1958
sources: Wikipedia, 'Second Taiwan Strait Crisis' (correcting the claim that Dulles authorized a public statement of nuclear readiness)

stops.name: Taipei, four days with the Generalissimo
stops.date_confidence: attested: Dulles at Taipei 20-23 October 1958
stops.campa: He flies to Taipei for four days at the end of October while the shelling continues on alternate days, an arrangement the two Chinese governments have settled into without agreeing to anything. What he takes away from Chiang Kai-shek is a communique renouncing the use of force as the principal means of returning to the mainland. It is the nearest thing to a concession the Generalissimo ever puts his name to. He has spent the five weeks before this trip refusing to say what the United States would do.
suggested_refs: The Dulles-Chiang communique of 23 October 1958

stops.name: Walter Reed, the cancer returns
stops.date_confidence: attested for February 1959; the day is not fixed by the sources reached and is a conventional placement
stops.campa: He goes back into Walter Reed in February for what is announced as a hernia operation. The surgeons open him and find the cancer returned and spread. He has been working through pain since the autumn, carrying it through a Berlin crisis in which Khrushchev has given the Western powers six months to get out of the city. He goes on working from the hospital, dictating and taking calls, with cables brought out from the department by courier. In the spring he crosses to Europe once more.
suggested_refs: The Berlin ultimatum of November 1958 and the crisis Dulles handled from a hospital bed
sources: Wikipedia, 'Walter Reed Army Medical Center' (coordinate correction)

stops.name: The State Department, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested: resignation 15 April 1959, formal termination of appointment recorded 22 April 1959
stops.campa: He resigns on the fifteenth of April, and the formal termination of the appointment is entered a week later. Six years and three months in the office, and he has held it more completely than any Secretary in living memory: Eisenhower let him run the department and most of the policy, and the two men spoke almost every day. Christian Herter, who walks on crutches from arthritis, takes the desk. Eisenhower keeps Dulles on as a consultant with cabinet rank.
suggested_refs: history.state.gov, termination of appointment recorded 22 April 1959

stops.name: Walter Reed, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies at Walter Reed on the morning of the twenty-fourth of May, seventy-one years old and five weeks out of office. The cancer has been in the bone since the winter. He had been Secretary of State for six years and three months and had spent the last two and a half of them under treatment for the disease that killed him, a fact known inside the government and little discussed outside it. The department is Herter's now. The Berlin foreign ministers' conference he had argued for is sitting in Geneva as he dies.

stops.name: Washington National Cathedral, the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The funeral is held in the cathedral on Mount Saint Alban with Eisenhower in the pews and the delegations of allied governments behind him, West Germany's among them. The son of the Watertown manse is buried out of a Protestant cathedral by a government, which is nearer to what his father wanted than either of them would have put it. He is given the Medal of Freedom posthumously, the civilian award Truman created in 1945; the Presidential Medal of Freedom he is often said to hold did not exist until 1963.

stops.name: Arlington, the grave near the grandfather
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the section and lot could not be confirmed, both the cemetery site and Find a Grave having blocked automated retrieval
stops.campa: He is buried at Arlington, across the river from the city whose foreign relations he directed, near the grave of John Watson Foster, the grandfather who held the same office sixty-seven years before him. Robert Lansing, the uncle who held it in between, lies at Watertown. Allen Dulles will not be laid here. In 1969 he goes to the family plot at Green Mount Cemetery in Baltimore, forty miles up the road. The section and lot of Foster's own grave are not confirmed in any record reached.

stops.name: West Berlin, a street on the frontier
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1959; the naming ceremony's month and day are not fixed by the sources reached
stops.campa: West Berlin makes a single avenue out of the old Zeltenallee and the Spreeweg and gives it his name, running from the Tiergarten past the Kongresshalle toward the Reichstag. His successor Christian Herter attends the dedication. Six months before, Khrushchev had given the Western powers an ultimatum to leave this city, and Dulles had answered that they would not. Two years after the ceremony a wall goes up a few hundred meters east of the street. The street keeps the name.

stops.name: Dulles, Virginia, the airport dedicated
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eisenhower had chosen the site himself in 1958, out in Virginia farmland where there was nothing, and after Dulles died he asked that the airport carry the name. Kennedy dedicates it on the seventeenth of November 1962, three weeks after the Cuban missile crisis, with Eisenhower on the platform beside him. Eero Saarinen's terminal is the last building he designed, and he did not live to see it open either: a concrete roof slung like a hammock between two rows of outward-leaning piers.

Note: no verified source was found for a statue or bust of Dulles in the terminal, and the claim should not be repeated

stops.name: Princeton, the papers in Firestone
stops.date_confidence: uncertain: the 1962 establishment date comes from a single secondary source and could not be verified, Princeton's finding-aid pages having returned 403 and bot-verification blocks
stops.campa: His papers go to the university he entered at sixteen, into a section of Firestone Library named the John Foster Dulles Library of Diplomatic History. The correspondence of the firm, the commission, and the department sits in one building. The operational record of what his brother's agency did in Tehran and in Guatemala sat in another and came out in pieces from the 1990s on. Historians read the two halves against each other. When the library was established is not confirmed: Princeton's finding aids could not be reached.
